schools.summary: Henry sets the whole speech under two heads, the lusts of the flesh and the love of the world, and reads the vow as a guard at the outermost gate: Job would not admit even a wanton look or thought, understanding the seventh commandment as Christ did (Matt. 5:28).
Gill takes the covenant with the eyes as a solemn engagement, in the strength of grace, not to gaze wantonly, since the eyes are the inlets to uncleanness.
Ellicott frames the chapter as one grand profession of innocence, clearing Job even of secret sins, the covenant made with the eyes as the avenues of desire.

Clarke renders 'I have cut the covenant sacrifice with my eyes' and alone reads 'a maid' (bethulah) as an idol, the Baithulia or anointed stones, so that Job purges himself of idolatry from the first line; Wesley: Job abstained from the least occasions of evil.

debates.question: Does the covenant of the eyes fence against lust, or against idolatry?

sides.position: against sensual desire — 'why then should I think upon a maid?' a vow of chastity in heart and eye
against idolatry — bethulah signifies an idol, the anointed stones (Baithulia)

outliers.note: Reads bethulah not as a maid but as an idol, the Baithulia or animated/anointed stones of Sanchoniathon and Bochart, making the opening line a renunciation of idolatry rather than of lust.

schools.summary: Gill: the impure can expect no good portion from the God who is above, for God himself is the portion of his people, and the vicious can claim no part in him.
Henry: uncleanness forfeits all good and shuts men out from the hope of it, for there is no portion or happiness for a soul but in God, and no unclean thing shall enter the New Jerusalem.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'the dispensation of Eloah from above, and the inheritance of the Almighty from the heights,' and note Job stands outside the Sinaitic revelation, his faith the old patriarchal 'religion of Abraham'; Ellicott compares Joseph's remonstrance (Gen. 39:9).
Clarke hears a note of grievance — what reward has he received?; Wesley: however secretly the unchaste act, one on a higher place sees how they act.

outliers.note: Pause to observe that Job is no Israelite but stands outside the positive Sinaitic revelation, his religion the old patriarchal faith still called din Ibrahim, the religion of Abraham or of the steppe — a frame governing the whole self-portrait.

themes: what portion of God from above

schools.summary: Gill: wickedness is the cause of destruction, swift and everlasting, laid up among the treasures of God's wrath, from which there is no deliverance but by Christ.

Henry hears 'destruction' and 'a strange punishment' as divine vengeance; fools mock the sin, but the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience (Eph. 5:6), and the destruction of Sodom is his instance of a strange punishment.
Keil and Delitzsch render parallel warnings, 'doth not calamity overtake the wicked'; Ellicott ties it tightly to the preceding verse — this destruction is simply the portion there named.
Clarke keeps his idolatry reading: would not such a secret hypocrite, an idolater under a show of faith, be marked by a strange and unheard-of punishment?

themes: the fear of judgment as a fence

schools.summary: Gill: God beholds all the ways of men; no darkness hides the workers of iniquity, and he counts every step, an argument that kept Job from secret uncleanness.
Henry finds two things before Job's eyes — God's omniscience (he sees our ways) and his observance (he counts our steps, even our by-steps into sin), for he will bring every work into judgment.
Ellicott lays the weight on the emphatic 'He,' plainly God, judge of the hearts and reins (Ps. 7:9; Jer. 17:10); Keil and Delitzsch carry the same all-seeing gaze from the preceding strophe.
Clarke puts it as impossibility: can Job suppose he could screen himself from the eye of God while guilty of such iniquities?

themes: doth not he see my ways

schools.summary: Gill weighs the senses of 'walked with vanity' — with vain men, or in vanity of mind, or most likely using deceitful methods to defraud, the vice Job now clears himself of.
Henry: Job never durst tell a lie to get a good bargain nor hasted to deceit; some men's constant walk is a constant cheat, but Job's wealth was not acquired by vanity.

Clarke reads 'vanity' (shav) as a false god, so that the clause renounces idolatry (Jer. 18:15; Hos. 12:11); Wesley glosses it as dealing with men in lying, and hasting to deceit as greedily seizing the chance to wrong others.

debates.question: Does 'walked with vanity' renounce fraud in trade or idolatry?

outliers.note: Continues his idolatrous construction of the passage, taking 'vanity' as the Hebrew shav, a false god, so that the whole discourse is a vindication from idolatrous practices.

schools.summary: Gill renders 'in balances of righteousness,' God's strict justice; put the weight of righteousness in one scale and Job's actions in the other, and the balance would hang even.
Henry: Job is willing to have his goods searched, sure they would weigh well and not, like Belshazzar's, be found too light — Tekel written on them (Dan. 5:27).
Keil and Delitzsch keep the forensic edge: the strophe is a string of self-imprecations governed by this wish to be weighed, that God may bring to light Job's integrity.
Clarke fixes tummathi, 'my perfection,' the totality of an unblameable life; Wesley reads it as an outright appeal, 'and he will know,' God finding out and owning his sincerity.

themes: that God may know mine integrity

schools.summary: Gill: Job never knowingly and of set purpose turned out of the way of righteousness, nor persisted when drawn aside, referring the clause especially to false dealing.
Henry takes the three members — steps never turned from justice, heart not walking after the eyes (the lust of the eye, 1 John 2:16, as Achan saw and took), no blot cleaving to the hands.

Keil and Delitzsch work the grammar — steps swerving, heart after the eyes, a spot (maum, macula, Dan. 1:4) on the hands, the 'offspring' here the produce of the ground; Ellicott calls the phrase emphatic, the narrow way, and compares 'the way' (Acts 9:2).
Clarke welcomes the scrutiny — 'I am willing to be sifted to the uttermost'; Wesley reads the heart after the eyes as letting it loose to covet what the eyes see, the blot any unjust gain.

themes: step turned out of the way

schools.summary: Gill reads the imprecation straight: if Job gained by fraud, let him sow and another eat, one of God's threatened judgments on the disobedient.

Henry: Job will forfeit the whole cargo if any contraband be found — 'let me sow, and let another eat' (the doom of oppressors, ch. 5:5), and his offspring be rooted out — staking the ruins of his estate on the trial.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'let another eat, and let my shoots be rooted out,' noting the saying has the ring of the proverb behind John 4:37, 'one soweth, and another reapeth.'
Clarke reads the double stroke on circumstances and family, noting it was probable not all Job's children perished in ch. 1:19; Wesley widens 'increase' to all his plants, fruits, and improvements.

themes: let me sow and another eat

schools.summary: Gill reads the heart deceived by another man's wife, through no fault of hers, but withstood by grace as Joseph withstood, though the wisest of men was drawn aside by such snares.
Henry takes coveting and contriving: Job did not covet his neighbour's wife (Prov. 7:6) nor lay wait at his door, and finds the fountain of all such sin in a deceived heart.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'befooled about a woman,' taking 'neighbour' as in the tenth commandment (Exod. 20:17); Job did not give his heart leave to trespass on a neighbour's marriage.
Clarke notes the Septuagint here supplies 'another man's wife,' fixing that it is adultery, not mere fancy, that Job disclaims.

themes: laid wait at the neighbour's door
the deceived heart the source of sin

schools.summary: Gill sets out both readings without choosing: 'let my wife grind unto another' as menial drudgery for a stranger, or figuratively that she lie with another and be defiled, the sense of the Targum and Aben Ezra.
Henry reports both — 'a slave, so some, a harlot, so others' — and draws the providence that God often punishes the sin of one with the sin of another, as in David's case (2 Sam. 12:11).
Keil and Delitzsch render 'grind unto another, and let others bow down over her,' passing to the ground of the curse; Ellicott glosses 'grind' as performing all menial offices, like a slave.

Clarke gives both a plain and a terrible reading — work at the handmill (Syriac, Arabic), and a bondwoman with no command of her own person; Wesley guards that Job did not desire this but would own God's justice in it.

debates.question: Is 'let my wife grind unto another' a curse of menial slavery or of adultery?

sides.position: literal — reduced to a slave's drudgery at the handmill
figurative — given up to defilement by another (Targum, Aben Ezra)

themes: let my wife grind unto another

schools.summary: Gill: adultery is contrary to the light of nature and the law of God, a breach of the marriage covenant that brings confusion into families, kingdoms, and states.

Henry heightens it as one of the greatest and vilest of sins, and marks that the magistrate ought to punish it, so adjudged in the patriarchal age before Moses made it capital, even when the guilty man is himself a judge.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'an infamous act... a crime to be brought before judges,' keeping the twofold guilt, shameful in itself and a matter for the tribunal.

Clarke cites Good's 'a premeditated crime, and a profligacy of the understanding,' a sin of the first magnitude against society; Wesley reads 'an iniquity of the judges,' punishable with death by the law of nature as by Moses.

Gill lets the fire play over its senses — burning lust, the rage of jealousy, the punishment by burning among the Canaanites, and the wrath of God that burns to the lowest hell, consuming soul and body.

Henry: lust is a fire in the soul that consumes the convictions and comforts, lays the conscience waste, kindles the fire of God's wrath, and roots out all the increase — perhaps with an eye to the burning of Sodom.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'a fire that consumeth to the abyss, and should root out all my increase,' the flame reaching downward to destruction and outward to the ruin of the estate.

Clarke: nothing is so destructive of domestic peace, for where jealousy exists unmixed misery dwells; Wesley echoes that lust consumes convictions, comforts, body, substance, and kindles God's unquenchable wrath.

themes: a fire that consumeth to destruction

schools.summary: Gill: whether the servants' quarrel was among themselves or against Job himself, over work, wages, food, or clothing, he did not reject it but searched into its merits and passed a righteous sentence.

Henry reads a rare condescension: Job heard his servants' reasons even when they contended with him, redressing their grievances — a great example to masters (Col. 4:1; Eph. 6:9) not to rule with a high hand.

Keil and Delitzsch note the maidservant is amah, not necessarily a slave, and that the Talmud rightly reads the servants as themselves beginning the dispute; Ellicott hears Job answering Eliphaz's charge (ch. 22:8), regarding servants as brethren in a common humanity.
Clarke sets the protest against the age's harsh law, in which slaves had no action at law; Job's boast is that he admitted his servants to all civil rights, ready to be pleaded against.

themes: the cause of manservant and maid
justice below the rank law required

schools.summary: Gill: had Job wronged his servants' cause, he would be at an utter loss when God rose to defend it, whether in providence or at the judgment where master and servant alike must answer.

Henry makes the thought the very curb on oppression: Job remembered a Master in heaven who will rise up and visit (Isa. 10:3), and, being undone if God were extreme to mark what we do amiss, we ought not to be rigorous with our inferiors.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'what should I do if God should rise up, and if He should make search, what should I answer Him?' — the question left for the next verse to answer in the common origin of master and man.

themes: what shall I do when God riseth up

schools.summary: Gill: though parents are the instruments, God is the maker of all, and master and servant alike are fashioned in the same shop of nature, the womb.
Henry hears the thought that curbed Job's harshness — 'have we not all one Father?' — and draws the rule of justice, parium par sit ratio, since men are of one mould, by one power, for one end.

Keil and Delitzsch argue 'one' is the subject and means the one God who made both (Mal. 2:10; cf. Eph. 6:9), the reading of the Targum, Jerome, and Saadia, against the Septuagint's adverbial 'in the same womb'; Ellicott hears the verse meeting Eliphaz (ch. 22:6).
Clarke reads Job's steady sense of a coming assize where king and slave stand on an equal footing, all civil distinctions abolished.

outliers.note: Take the disputed 'one' (echad) as the subject meaning the one God who fashioned master and servant, against the Septuagint and Symmachus, who construe it adverbially, 'in the same womb.'

themes: master and servant one in creation
have we not all one Father

schools.summary: Gill measures the protest: Job denied the poor no reasonable desire in his power to grant, a piece of bread or clothing, though not their unbounded wishes.
Henry recalls Eliphaz's charge (ch. 22:6) that Job stripped the naked and sent widows empty, and finds it false: Job granted the poor their desire and never caused the widow's craving eye to fail.

Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of a long hypothetical period reaching to the imprecation of v.22, rendering 'if I held back the poor from what they desired, and caused the eyes of the widow to languish.'

Wesley glosses withholding the poor as denying what they sought, and the widow's failing eyes as wearing her out with tedious expectation; Job is most large here because Eliphaz accused him most in this matter.

themes: withholding the poor from their desire

schools.summary: Gill: though Job kept a plentiful table he calls his provision a 'morsel,' and he did not eat it alone but shared with the poor the same meat he ate.
Henry lifts the act into an honour done the poor: Job took the fatherless to eat at his own table, of the best dish and not the crumbs, as David took Mephibosheth.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the clause within the running oath of Job's care for the helpless, of a piece with clothing the naked and guiding the widow.
Clarke sets it against ancient hospitality, deriving coena from koinonia (fellowship), yet notes Job speaks of the humbler, better thing — dividing his bread with the hungry.
Gill reads it of Job's early fatherly compassion: from his youth the fatherless was brought up with him as with a father.
Henry expands it to fatherless and widow both — a father to the orphan, a guide to the widow who had lost the guide of her youth — and traces the tenderness to Job's own upbringing.
Ellicott settles the hard pronouns: 'he' is the fatherless of v.17 and 'her' the widow of v.16, so the orphan grew up under Job's care and the widow was guided by him.

Wesley reads 'from my youth' as from when Job could manage his affairs, and 'her' as the widow guided with a father's tenderness; Clarke throws up his hands at the diversity of renderings — Heath, Houbigant, Good, Coverdale, the Septuagint, the Syriac — asking 'who can reconcile such discordant translations?'

outliers.note: Lays six widely divergent renderings of the verse side by side (Heath, Houbigant, Good, Coverdale, Septuagint, Syriac) and confesses it a genuine, unresolved crux — 'who can reconcile such discordant translations?'

schools.summary: Gill: Job does not deny seeing men perish for want of clothing, but denies ever seeing them so as to despise or overlook them without provision.
Henry marks that clothing costs more than feeding: instead of rich liveries for his servants while the poor went in rags, Job had warm clothing made of his own fleece.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'one perishing without clothing' and fix the participle — one come down from his place and going to ruin; Ellicott offers the alternative 'any wanderer without,' the shelterless vagrant.

themes: any perish for want of clothing

schools.summary: Gill: the poor man's loins, girded with the garment Job gave, blessed him, moving Job to a wish of happiness on the man he clothed.
Henry: the warmed poor blessed Job and blessed God for him; his sheep were later burned with fire from heaven, but while he had them he used them charitably.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'if his loins blessed me not, and he did not warm himself from the hide of my lambs,' one more clause in the great hypothetical period awaiting its imprecation at v.22.
Clarke calls it a very delicate touch — the part once cold, now warm, made by a fine prosopopoeia to bless the giver.
Gill unfolds 'lifted up my hand' as menacing, or striking, or signalling others (as Ananias bade men smite Paul, Acts 23:2), or voting wrongly — none of which Job did.
Henry lays the stress on 'when I saw my help in the gate': Job never used his power to crush the weak, though he had interest enough in people and judges to do it unpunished.

Wesley fixes the phrase — 'when I saw I could influence the judges'; Clarke reaches for a parallel in Lebeid's poem (in Sir William Jones's version) of the just desert chief who relinquishes his own right to establish the poor's.

themes: lifting the hand against the fatherless

schools.summary: Gill wishes the very limb disjointed, in just retaliation for lifting it against the weak, as Jeroboam's arm withered against the man of God (1 Kings 13:4); Eliphaz had charged Job with breaking the arms of the fatherless (ch. 22:9).
Henry: had Job not been clear he durst not have challenged the divine vengeance; it is righteous with God to break the arm lifted against the fatherless, as he withered Jeroboam's.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'let my shoulder fall out of its shoulder-blade,' the delayed apodosis to the whole long series of conditions.
Clarke prefers Good's anatomical rendering, 'my shoulder-bone shivered at the blade,' letting judgment fall on the very parts that did wrong.

themes: let mine arm fall from the shoulder

schools.summary: Gill: Job feared not men, at his command, but God; the dread of destruction, temporal and eternal, kept him from all injustice, though as one who knew his Redeemer he chiefly feared temporal ruin and a Father's chastening.

Henry sets the terror under two heads — the majesty of God (his highness, the infinite distance, Eccl. 5:8) and the wrath of God — and draws that even the best need to restrain themselves with the fear of destruction, as Adam in innocency was awed by a threatening.
Clarke: preserved from sin through the fear of God's judgments, never daring his Judge's anger in his Judge's eye; Wesley: Job knew himself unable to oppose God's power or bear his wrath.
Ellicott corrects 'I could not endure' to 'I was unable to act thus' — the majesty of God made the wrong itself impossible, not merely its consequence unbearable.

themes: fear as the keeper of mercy

schools.summary: Gill: covetousness is idolatry, the covetous man worshipping his gold; to make gold one's hope is to set it in God's room, whereas the good man hopes not for gold on earth but glory in heaven.

Henry: Job had gold, even fine gold, yet put no confidence in it, for it is hard to have riches and not trust them, which is what makes it so difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom (Matt. 19:23).
Clarke attends to the two words for gold, zahab (polished) and kethem (stamped), referring to his fuller note at ch. 28:15-17.
Ellicott hears the verse answering Eliphaz, who had bidden Job lay up gold as dust and make the Almighty his defence (ch. 22:23-24).

themes: trust in wealth or in God

schools.summary: Gill: Job disclaims not all gladness but the carnal, self-pleasing joy that forgets the giver; a man may lawfully rejoice in God's goodness in increasing his substance.

Henry: Job took no pride in his wealth nor thought his own hand had gotten it (Deut. 8:17), never saying with the fool 'Soul, take thine ease' (Luke 12:19); his moderate joy in gaining steadied him in losing.
Keil and Delitzsch set the couplet at the head of the strophe running to sun-worship, the heart's over-valuing of gold of a piece with the eye's temptation to worship the hosts of heaven.
Gill canvasses the readings but concludes it means the literal worship of sun and moon, the first idolatry.
Henry: the most ancient idolatry (Deut. 4:19), then practised secretly; Job never beheld the lights but to look through them by faith to the Father of lights.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'the sunlight when it shone, and the moon walking in splendour'; Ellicott observes Job repudiates only sun and moon worship, seeming to know nothing of the grosser kinds — a mark of his primitive religion.

Clarke names it Sabaeism, the worship of the heavenly bodies, following Calmet's three points (worshipping sun/moon, adoring at rising/change, kissing the hand); Wesley: the worship of the host of heaven, most ancient and most frequent in the East.

outliers.note: Remarks that Job repudiates only sun- and moon-worship and seems ignorant of the grosser, more degraded kinds of idolatry — a sign of the pure and primitive character of his religion.

themes: looking through the light to its Maker

schools.summary: Gill: the heart drawn by the glory of the lights to think them deities and worship them privately — a secret idolatry of the heart, in the chambers of imagery (Ezek. 8:12).

Henry sets heart and hand together: Job kept his heart from being enticed to think there was a divine glory in the lights (idolatry begins in the heart, drawn away by lust, Jas. 1:14), and his mouth never kissed his hand.

Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the gesture — the kiss of the hand as the proskynesis or adoratio of the ancients, citing Pliny and Tacitus, kin to kissing the calves (Hos. 13:2); the verb 'enticed' as in Deut. 11:16.
Gill: an iniquity for the magistrates, God's vicegerents; the Mosaic law punished it by stoning, and the idolater's portion is the lake of fire (Rev. 21:8).

Henry sets its two faces — an affront to the magistrate, a public nuisance, and a far greater affront to God, high treason: 'I should have denied the God that is above,' for idolatry is in effect atheism (Eph. 2:12).

Clarke: had Job adored them he would have denied the God that made them; Wesley reads 'the judge' as the civil magistrate obliged to vindicate God's honour, the denial being by consequence, robbing God of his prerogative.
Ellicott would render 'by my judge,' meaning God, doubting any reference to the Mosaic law (Deut. 17:2-7).

debates.question: Is 'punished by the judge' the civil magistrate or God?

sides.position: the civil magistrate, God's vicegerent, bound to punish idolatry

schools.summary: Gill: Job had enemies, hated for his goodness, on whom calamity fell; the wicked rejoice in an enemy's adversity, but good men should not, though it requires a large measure of grace not to feel the secret pleasure.
Henry: Job did not so much as rejoice when mischief befell those who hated him, remembering that to do so would bring the destruction on himself (Prov. 24:17-18).

Keil and Delitzsch note the broken construction, an aposiopesis equal to a solemn denial; Ellicott observes how much deeper Job searches than his accusers, entering the realm of the wishes and thoughts.
Clarke states it as fact: 'I did not avenge myself on my enemy; I neither bore malice nor hatred to him.'

themes: the realm of wishes and thoughts

schools.summary: Gill: Job laid an embargo on his tongue and kept it bridled from cursing his adversaries — a hard restraint when provocations are given.
Henry joins it to the verse before: Job never wished a curse to their soul (the worst of curses) nor desired their death, careful not to offend with his tongue (Ps. 39:1).
Keil and Delitzsch render 'I did not allow my palate to sin by calling down a curse upon his life,' the simple negative completing the broken oath of the preceding line.
Clarke: 'I have neither spoken evil of him, nor wished evil to him' — adding how few called Christians can say the same of their enemies.

themes: not suffering my mouth to sin
the curse withheld from the enemy

schools.summary: Gill takes 'the men of my tabernacle' for Job's friends or, more likely, his domestic servants, leaving the sense of their saying open.

Henry reads them so enraged at their master's enemy that they could have eaten him had Job set them on, showing how beloved he was, yet how strict a hand he kept on his own passions (as David had those about him, 1 Sam. 24:4).

Wesley: the domestics so zealous in Job's quarrel they could eat the enemy's flesh, yet he restrained them and himself; Clarke, following the Targum, turns it the opposite way — the servants owning that their master's own meat was freely shared, none unsatisfied with his flesh.
Ellicott keeps the revenge construction, 'oh that we had of his flesh! we should never be satisfied,' comparing ch. 19:22.

debates.question: Do the men of Job's tent thirst for the enemy's flesh, or testify to Job's bounty?

sides.position: servants zealous for revenge, wishing the enemy's flesh, whom Job restrained
servants testifying that none went unsatisfied with Job's own meat (the Targum)

themes: the enemy's flesh or the master's bounty

schools.summary: Gill: the stranger, one out of his country, Job never suffered to lie in the street through the night, exposed to the weather, but took in.

Henry hears the whole law of hospitality — the stranger not lodging in the street as angels might have in Sodom but for Lot (Heb. 13:2) — Job opening his door to the road as Abraham in his tent-door (Gen. 18:1).

Keil and Delitzsch render 'the stranger did not lodge out of doors, I opened my door towards the street'; Ellicott finds the manners of Gen. 19:2-3 and Judg. 19:20-21, 'the traveller' being literally the road, the wayfarer.
Clarke: the kindness reached not merely family and friends but the perfectly unknown and the traveller, refreshed with Job's bed and board.

themes: the stranger not lodging in the street
hospitality as the crown of charity

schools.summary: Gill: Job does not claim sinlessness but denies covering his sins as Adam did, laying blame on his wife, or as men commonly do through fear or shame.
Henry hears Job answering Zophar (ch. 20:12): he never made fig-leaves the shelter of his shame nor hid iniquity in his bosom, for he that covers his sins shall not prosper (Prov. 28:13).

Keil and Delitzsch argue strongly for 'like Adam' rather than 'after the manner of men,' the force of Hos. 6:7 lying in the comparison to the first man's transgression; Ellicott holds it open, 'as Adam, or as man.'
Clarke finds an evident allusion to the Fall, unfolding Adam's threefold concealment; Wesley reads it flatly, 'as Adam did in Paradise.'

debates.question: Does 'as Adam' name the man Adam and the Fall, or mankind generally?

sides.position: the man Adam — an allusion to the Fall (cf. Hos. 6:7)
'as men' commonly do — the sense held open

schools.summary: Gill: no fear of men ever deterred Job from confessing his fault publicly when conscience required it.
Henry makes Job's courage the proof of his sincerity: a man of undaunted resolution who boldly defended religion and justice, fearing the great God and his curse, not the multitude and its scorn.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the connecting force: the verse denies the motive for hiding sin — Job did not dread the people's judgment or the stigma of the families so as to keep silent and retired.

Wesley: Job durst not keep silence or stay within when called to act for God; Clarke asks whether Job was ever put in fear from judging rightly, and notes Good's alternative that turns the verse into a self-imprecation.

outliers.note: Notes Good's rendering that recasts the verse as a self-imprecation — 'then let me be confounded before the assembled multitude... let me be struck dumb' — should Job have done the evils just named.

themes: did I fear a great multitude

schools.summary: Gill renders 'who will give me a hearer?' — not an idle listener but one to hear his cause pleaded in a judicial way, and above all God himself.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'behold my signature — the Almighty will answer me — and the writing which my opponent hath written,' rejecting the sense 'let my adversary write a book'; Ellicott agrees, 'here is my mark,' and notes the disturbed order, vv.35-37 properly following the imprecation on the land.

Clarke: 'there is my pledge' (hen tavi), Job binding himself to trial and desiring his accuser to draw up a proper bill of indictment; Wesley reads 'had written a book' of a charge in writing, inferring Job did not live before letters were in use.

outliers.note: Infers from 'that mine adversary had written a book' that Job did not live before letters were in use, the first letters being those written by the finger of God on the two tables.

themes: oh that one would hear me
that mine adversary had written a book

schools.summary: Gill unfolds 'take it upon my shoulder' as bearing the charge lightly, or confessing openly, or carrying it as an honour, like a sceptre or the sword of state, and binding it as a crown.
Henry: an upright heart does not dread a scrutiny; Job would wear the indictment as an ornament, glad to learn any hidden sin or to disprove a false charge and come off with the more honour.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'I will carry it upon my shoulder, I will wind it about me as a crown,' the bearing of a man sure of acquittal.
Clarke enriches it from a book of Chinese punishments, in which the crime is written on a board worn about the neck; Job would clasp such a board as a crown, sure his innocence would appear.

themes: taking the indictment on the shoulder
the charge worn as an ornament

schools.summary: Gill: Job would give his judge a full narrative of his life — not that God needs it, but to show how little he feared the closest examination of his ways.
Henry: the defendant ready to give his accusers all fair play, and so confident that, as a prince to be crowned rather than a prisoner tried, he would go near to God.

Clarke: Job would show every station and office of his life and approach as the nagid, the sovereign chief, gathering the passage into a fivefold desire for trial; Wesley glosses 'as a prince' as undaunted courage and confidence.
Ellicott owns the sense uncertain — either giving a ready account with alacrity, or meeting God as one meets a prince, with deference — and sets against it the roll of names the friends flung at Job.

themes: declaring the number of my steps
the confidence of a clear conscience

schools.summary: Gill notes some would move these closing verses earlier but keeps the received order, reading Job clearing himself of oppression: his land did not cry out as unjustly gotten or ill-used.
Henry: Job's estate was got and used honestly, so his land and furrows could not complain as they do against those who gain by extortion, over whom the stone cries from the wall (Hab. 2:9-11).

Clarke states plainly the verses are out of their place and disturb the connection, referring Job's meaning to the sabbath of the land (Lev. 25:1-7); Wesley reads the cry of the land 'because I have gotten it by fraud or violence.'
Ellicott renders 'if the furrows thereof weep together,' a bold impersonation, and observes Job has far more than traversed the indictment, showing himself perfect and upright.

debates.question: Do vv.38-40 stand in their proper place, or belong earlier (Job's words ending at v.37)?

sides.position: displaced — they disturb the connection and belong after v.25 or v.37

themes: if my land cry against me
oppression and the sabbath of the land

schools.summary: Gill: Job ate nothing of his land's increase without paying — not got the fields by deceit or force, nor failed to pay ploughmen and reapers or his tenants their price.

Henry names the two things Job could safely say: he paid for what he bought, as Abraham (Gen. 23:16) and David (2 Sam. 24:24), and never caused an owner to lose his life, as Ahab got Naboth's vineyard.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'if I have devoured its strength without payment, and caused the soul of its possessor to expire,' adding the note that here 'the words of Job are ended.'

Clarke: Job was never the narrow-minded man who exhausts his land or defrauds his workers, noting Coverdale's 'if I have grieved any of the plowmen'; Wesley glosses the owner's lost life as killing him for undisturbed possession, as Ahab did.
Gill reads the imprecation straight — thistles for wheat, noxious weeds for barley, an echo of the original curse, a judgment God sometimes executes on a land for its dwellers' wickedness.

Henry draws the moral — the unjust estate yields thistles for wheat — and on 'the words of Job are ended' marks that Job closes his defence in triumph, keeping the field: 'who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect?' (Rom. 8:33).

Clarke works the plant-names (choach a hooked thorn, boshah a fetid, poisonous weed) and judges 'the words of Job are ended' a likely later addition, wanting in many manuscripts, which Coverdale set off as a rubric — following Kennicott's reordering of the appeal as the true climax.

outliers.note: Judges the closing clause 'the words of Job are ended' a likely scribal addition of no authority, wanting in many manuscripts and standing detached in the Hebrew, which Coverdale set off in a separate rubric line.

themes: the words of Job are ended
